title: Lexical scope and the scope chain
hook: Scope is not about where code runs — it is about where code was written. The scope chain is a linked list of environments the engine walks to resolve a variable name, and it is separate from the call stack.

blocks.text: **Lexical scope** (also called static scope) means a function can access variables declared in its outer blocks based on source text position, not based on who called it. Each scope creates an **environment** (variable bindings). The **scope chain** links inner environments to outer ones through the `[[Environment]]` internal slot on functions. `var` is function-scoped; `let` and `const` are block-scoped. Global scope is the outermost link.

entries.plainDefinition: Variable visibility determined by where functions and blocks are written in source code.
entries.example: function outer() { const x = 1; function inner() { console.log(x); } }

entries.plainDefinition: The chain of outer lexical environments consulted when resolving an identifier.
Bindings created by let, const, class, or {} that exist only inside the block.
entries.example: if (true) { let x = 1; } // x not visible outside

entries.plainDefinition: Bindings created by var and function declarations inside a function body.

blocks.text: Understanding scope chain vs call stack is a top Reddit and FAANG interview topic. The call stack tracks *which function is running now*; the scope chain tracks *which environments are visible to that function*. A nested function always sees the environment where it was defined, even if invoked from elsewhere. Block scope with `let`/`const` prevents accidental leakage from `if`, `for`, and `try` blocks — and fixes the classic loop-with-`var` trap covered in the closures topic.

blocks.title: Scope chain ≠ call stack
blocks.body: Calling a function from another file does not change its scope chain. Only the lexical nesting at definition time matters.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Start in current environment
items.body: Look up the name in the innermost lexical environment (function params, block locals).

items.title: Walk the scope chain
items.body: If not found, follow the outer reference to the parent environment until global or module scope.

items.title: ReferenceError if missing
items.body: If no binding exists on the chain, throw ReferenceError (not undefined unless you declared let x without assigning).

items.title: Separate from call stack
items.body: The executing frame's scope comes from [[Environment]], not from who invoked the function.

  end

blocks.title: Assuming dynamic scope
blocks.body: JavaScript is not Perl — inner functions do not see the caller's locals. Only lexical outer environments count.

blocks.title: Using var in blocks expecting isolation
blocks.body: for (var i = 0; ...) leaks i outside the loop. Prefer let for loop counters and block-scoped temporaries.

interviewTakeaways: Lexical scope is fixed at write time; the scope chain is the linked list of outer environments.
Call stack = execution order; scope chain = variable visibility — interviewers love contrasting these.
let/const are block-scoped; var is function-scoped and hoisted without initialization until assignment.
60s: Resolve names by walking outer environments from inner to global. Where a function is defined sets its chain, not where it is called.
Follow-up: what is the Temporal Dead Zone for let/const?
commonPitfalls: Confusing scope chain with call stack — calling from elsewhere does not change visible variables.
Using var inside loops and expecting per-iteration bindings — leads to the closure loop trap.
Strong answer: 'Scope is lexical. Each function carries [[Environment]]. Lookup walks outward. Block scope with let fixes loop capture bugs.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: TypeScript respects the same scope rules at type-check time. Unused block locals can trigger noUnusedLocals.
C# nested methods (local functions) also close over outer locals lexically. No var/function-scope split — all locals are block-scoped.
